articles.title: BepiColombo begins Mercury arrival with MTM separation success
articles.description: On 3 September 2026 at 15:49 CEST, the European Space Agency's BepiColombo Mission Control Team at the European Space Operations Centre (ESOC) received the signal they had been waiting for – BepiColombo’s Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) successfully separated from the spacecraft stack. This landmark achievement for the ESA and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) mission marks the first step of BepiColombo's long-awaited arrival at Mercury.
articles.summary: BepiColombo successfully completes its Mercury Thermostat Module separation on September 3, 2026, marking the beginning of the historic arrival sequence at Mercury. This critical maneuver represents a major milestone in ESA and JAXA's collaborative mission to study our solar system's innermost planet.

articles.title: Astronomers discover a radio galaxy with evidence of four separate jet outbursts
articles.description: Astronomers have identified what may be the first example of a new class of radio galaxy, one whose central black hole appears to have launched powerful jets on four separate occasions. High-resolution observations with the upgraded Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope (GMRT), combined with data from MeerKAT and the Very Large Array, reveal four pairs of radio structures arranged symmetrically around the central galaxy.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Astronomers discover a rare radio galaxy showing evidence of four distinct jet outbursts from its central black hole, potentially representing a new class of astronomical objects.

articles.title: Great news from Saturn's moon Enceladus in the search for life in space
articles.description: What are the chances of finding extraterrestrial life in our solar system? Frank Postberg, a professor of planetary science at Freie Universität Berlin, has published a study in Science Advances with an international team of researchers. They present new evidence that it is easier to determine the constituents of the ocean hidden beneath Enceladus's icy surface than previously assumed.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: New discoveries on Saturn's moon Enceladus strengthen evidence for conditions favorable to extraterrestrial life within our solar system.

articles.title: “We found something never seen before” – A dead star is producing a shock wave that shouldn’t exist
articles.description: A dead white dwarf with no detectable disk has somehow produced a powerful shock wave that appears to have persisted for at least 1,000 years. Its magnetic field may be partly responsible, but astronomers say an unexplained “mystery engine” may also be at work.
articles.summary: Astronomers discover a white dwarf generating a mysterious and powerful shock wave with no visible disk, revealing an unexpected stellar phenomenon.

articles.title: The Universe Is Full of Tiny Red Dots—and They’re One of Astronomy’s Biggest Discoveries in Decades
articles.description: A new type of object found in the early universe has puzzled astronomers for years, but they may finally have some answers.
articles.summary: Researchers have identified and explained mysterious 'tiny red dots' observed in the early universe, a major discovery that challenges previous models of galaxy formation. This breakthrough represents one of astronomy's most significant advances in recent decades.

articles.title: Astronomers Confirm Youngest Known Planet, Less Than 1 Million Years Old
articles.description: Astronomers have confirmed the youngest known planet yet, a Jupiter-size world less than 1 million years old that orbits a star about 450 light-years from Earth, according to a study published Sept. 16 in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. The planet, designa…
articles.summary: Astronomers confirm discovery of the youngest known planet ever detected—a Jupiter-sized world less than 1 million years old still forming around its star. This remarkable find provides unprecedented insights into planetary formation processes during their earliest stages.

articles.title: SpaceX Clears Launch Rehearsal Ahead of Starship’s First Orbital Attempt
articles.description:
During this milestone test, Starship will circle the Earth six times over ten hours at an altitude of 171 miles before touching down.
The post SpaceX Clears Launch Rehearsal Ahead of Starship’s First Orbital Attempt first appeared on Le·gal In·sur·rec·tion.
articles.summary: SpaceX clears critical launch rehearsal for Starship's first full orbital attempt, which will circle Earth six times at 171 miles altitude. This milestone test represents a major step toward operational space transportation.

articles.title: PRIMA, el futuro telescopio espacial de infrarrojo lejano de la NASA
articles.description:
La NASA acaba de lanzar el telescopio espacial Nancy Grace Roman, pero ya planea el siguiente. En 2033, si no hay retrasos, despegará PRIMA, un nuevo telescopio espacial para observar […]
La entrada PRIMA, el futuro telescopio espacial de infrarrojo lejano de…
articles.summary: NASA announces PRIMA, an ambitious far-infrared space telescope planned for 2033 to explore the history and evolution of the universe. The mission represents the next generation of flagship observatories following the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.

articles.title: NASA Selects Far-Infrared Telescope as First in New Mission Class
articles.description: NASA announced Wednesday a mission to explore the history and evolution of the universe, PRIMA (PRobe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics), is advancing to the next phase of development. This space telescope is the first in a new class of NASA astrophysics …
articles.summary: NASA selects PRIMA (PRobe far-Infrared Mission) as the inaugural mission in a new class dedicated to exploring the universe's history and evolution. The mission marks a significant commitment to far-infrared astronomy.

articles.title: Win a trip to ESA to witness BepiColombo arrive at Mercury
articles.description:
Get ready to celebrate BepiColombo’s arrival at Mercury. Craft a welcoming message that could be a drawing, song, poem or any other art form and stand a chance to win a trip to mission control! 
ENTRY FORM  
Full rules and how to enter below.
articles.summary: ESA invites the public to celebrate BepiColombo's historic arrival at Mercury with creative submissions. This landmark mission marks a major achievement in exploring our solar system's innermost planet.

articles.title: Juice to fly past Earth for third gravity assist
articles.description: The European Space Agency’s Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer (Juice) will return to Earth on 28 September, with flight controllers guiding the spacecraft close to our home planet to alter its speed and direction en route to Jupiter.
articles.summary: The European Space Agency's Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer (Juice) will perform its third gravity assist maneuver using Earth on September 28. This critical flyby helps redirect the spacecraft toward its mission to study Jupiter's icy moons.

articles.title: Webb reveals stunning panorama of star formation
articles.description: This starry view of the nearby star-forming region IC 348 is one of the largest images from the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope released to the public so far. Using Webb, astronomers searched IC 348 for brown dwarfs, which are less massive than the smallest stars. The researchers discovered brown dwarfs just twice the mass of Jupiter, bringing the study of these curious objects into a new mass range.
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope reveals a panoramic view of star formation in the nearby region IC 348. This expansive image demonstrates Webb's unprecedented capability to capture the beauty and complexity of stellar birth.

articles.title: BepiColombo’s Mercury arrival begins - full replay
articles.description:
Video: 
			02:31:10
				
Watch the replay of the livestream originally broadcast on 3 September as ESA/JAXA's BepiColombo mission took the first critical step towards arriving at Mercury.
After travelling through the inner Solar System together for eight years, BepiColombo's Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) will separate from the rest of the stacked spacecraft on 3 September 2026. This marks the beginning of one of the most complex planetary arrival sequences ever attempted by ESA.
Broadcast live from ESA's European Space Operations Centre (ESOC) in Darmstadt, Germany, the programme includes live views from the iconic Main Control Room, expert analysis, behind-the-scenes insights, and the first signal from the spacecraft following separation. 
Livestream schedule (CEST): 

13:45 – Livestream begins 
16:00-16:45 – End of livestream
articles.summary: ESA and JAXA's BepiColombo mission begins its Mercury arrival sequence, captured in a full livestream replay. This historic moment showcases humanity's continued exploration of the inner solar system.

articles.title: Astronomers Couldn't Explain This Ancient Star's Chemistry. A Lab Experiment Just Did.
articles.description: Everything from the gold in your smart phone to the calcium in your bones was originally created in a star. But for a long time there has been a question about the levels of one particular element - strontium, which makes fireworks burn bright red and is used in glow-in-the-dark paint. A new paper published in Nature Communications Physics from a large group of researchers led by Caley M. Harris, a graduate student at Michigan State University, thinks they have found an answer for why that particular elemental level was skewed - and doing so required some very elaborate laboratory testing.
articles.summary: A groundbreaking lab experiment finally explains the unusual chemistry of an ancient star, revealing how heavy elements are forged in stellar processes. This discovery enhances our understanding of stellar nucleosynthesis and the origins of elements in the universe.

articles.title: The Solar System’s First Planets Were Made of Fire, Not Ice
articles.description: The early stages of the solar system remain shrouded in mystery. Not much remains from that time, but scientists have developed plenty of theories about what was going on back then. One of those theories attempts to answer a simple question - did the early system prefer “fire” or “ice”? A new paper published in Nature Astrophysics from lead author Damanveer Grewal, an assistant professor of Earth and planetary sciences at Yale, and his co-authors, have a definitive answer to that question - the early solar system preferred fire.
articles.summary: New research reveals that the early solar system's planets formed from fiery, rocky materials rather than ice. This discovery reshapes our understanding of planetary formation and the evolution of our cosmic neighborhood.

articles.title: JWST Finds Dynamic Structural Evolution in Chariklo’s Rings
articles.description: When we think of asteroids, we often think of the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter that contains the majority of the known asteroids in our solar system. However, our solar system hosts several other populations of asteroids and icy rocks, including the Jupiter Trojan asteroids that orbit in Jupiter’s orbit, and the icy bodies and comets of the Kuiper Belt. But there’s one population of asteroids that often gets overlooked called Centaurs, primarily because their orbits are not in a fixed location and instead whose orbits cross the orbits of the outer planets.
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope discovers dynamic structural evolution in the rings of the asteroid Chariklo. This surprising finding reveals previously unknown complexity in small solar system bodies.

articles.title: Astronomers Find a Sub-Neptune Orbiting Completely Backward Around a Red Dwarf
articles.description: In our own solar system, all eight planets orbit our Sun in a nice, orderly fashion. None are more than 7° or so out of alignment with the equator, and all of them rotate in the same direction as the Sun itself. But that’s not the case for all solar systems, and a new paper published in Astronomy & Astrophysics from a team of researchers led by Yann Carteret, a PhD student at the University of Geneva (UNIGE), describes the first time we’ve ever found an exoplanet orbiting the opposite direction of its red dwarf parent star - and it has major implications for our understanding of planet formation theory.
articles.summary: Astronomers discover a remarkable sub-Neptune exoplanet orbiting backward around a red dwarf star, defying typical orbital patterns. This unusual configuration provides new insights into diverse planetary formation and migration mechanisms across the universe.

articles.title: Perseverance Reveals How Complex Water Systems Shaped the Jezero Crater on Early Mars
articles.description: A new study reveals that Jezero Crater’s enigmatic ‘Margin Unit’ was shaped by a complex sequence of ancient lakes, groundwater systems, and hydrothermal fluids.
articles.summary: The Perseverance rover reveals that Jezero Crater's complex geology was shaped by ancient lakes, groundwater, and mineral-rich waters. This discovery deepens our understanding of early Mars' habitability and water systems.

articles.title: Stanford Engineers Teach Spacecraft to "Dream" Their Way to the Space Station
articles.description: Docking with the ISS may seem simple. However, actually doing so is a showcase in how difficult orbital mechanics can be. It’s equivalent to traveling down a highway at 28,000 km/hr and parallel parking into an open garage on a multi-billion dollar laboratory traveling at the same speed. If you try to accelerate forward you actually drift up, and there’s no air friction to naturally slow you down. Oh, and if you hit the lab, everyone onboard both your craft and the station dies, and the resultant debris field could both wipe out dozens of satellites and even people on the ground. No pressure, obviously. For decades, aerospace engineers have been docking successfully using hard coded physics equations and human pilots to correct them. But now, a new paper, available in pre-print on arXiv from researchers at Stanford, is taking a shot at building an AI to perform a series of “mental simulations” that could fundamentally change how future spacecraft interact with each other.
articles.summary: Stanford engineers develop AI that enables spacecraft to autonomously navigate complex orbital mechanics for ISS docking by learning and adapting in real-time.

articles.title: Black hole jets reach far beyond galaxies' visible edges, potentially deciding their fate
articles.description: Galaxies are enormous and hold hundreds of billions of stars. These stars form from cold, dense gas. Every large galaxy, including the Milky Way, is wrapped in a huge envelope of gas called the circumgalactic medium, or CGM. This reservoir of raw material stretches 10–20 times the size of the visible portion of the galaxy.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Research reveals that black hole jets extend far beyond galaxy boundaries and play a crucial role in determining galactic evolution and fate.

articles.title: A real-time look inside spacecraft heat shields during extreme heat conditions
articles.description: When a spacecraft reenters Earth's atmosphere at hypersonic velocities, its protective heat shield faces extreme conditions, including temperatures beyond 3,000 degrees Fahrenheit (1,650 degrees Celsius). To survive, the shield relies on specialized materials that absorb heat as they degrade in a controlled process called ablation, sacrificing the shield's outer layers to protect the vehicle and crew within.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Scientists conduct breakthrough real-time observations of spacecraft heat shields during hypersonic reentry, advancing understanding of thermal protection systems.

articles.title: Webb detects ammonia and unexpected chill on a distant giant planet
articles.description: Using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), a team of astronomers led by the University of Maryland identified water, methane and ammonia in the atmosphere of HATS-6 b, a giant planet 500 light-years from Earth. The observations also revealed that HATS-6 b may be significantly cooler than standard calculations predict—suggesting that the planet's relationship with its star may be far more complicated than previously thought.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope detects ammonia and unexpected temperature conditions on a distant giant exoplanet, revealing surprising atmospheric properties.

articles.title: The secret to growing food on Mars could be fungi
articles.description: Scientists think beneficial fungi could help transform nutrient-poor lunar and Martian regolith into a material capable of supporting crops. By helping plants access nutrients and withstand harsh conditions, these microbes could someday make self-sustaining space farming more realistic.
articles.summary: Scientists identify beneficial fungi as a promising solution for converting nutrient-poor regolith into viable growing medium for food production on Mars and the Moon.

articles.title: Ancient meteorites reveal a powerful force that helped build the Solar System
articles.description: Ancient grains inside one of the oldest known meteorites reveal that a surprisingly strong magnetic field existed during the solar system’s first 200,000 years. The discovery suggests magnetism worked alongside gravity to help transform a vast cloud of gas and dust into the sun and planetary disk.
articles.summary: Ancient meteorite grains reveal that a surprisingly strong magnetic field existed in the early solar system, playing a key role in planetary formation.

articles.title: “We just need to go back” – Uranus’ moon Ariel may have hidden a 100-mile-deep ocean
articles.description: Ariel, one of Uranus’ moons, may once have contained a subsurface ocean more than 100 miles deep beneath its fractured icy shell. The finding, combined with similar evidence from Miranda, suggests the distant Uranian system could harbor multiple hidden ocean worlds.
articles.summary: New research suggests Uranus' moon Ariel may harbor a subsurface ocean exceeding 100 miles deep, opening possibilities for future exploration and discovery.

articles.title: These massive stars could explain Webb’s strangest galaxies
articles.description: Hubble observations of massive stars in metal-poor dwarf galaxies are revealing clues to why the early universe looks so unusual. Researchers found that stellar winds weaken sharply at extremely low metallicities, potentially allowing massive stars to retain more material and evolve in unexpected ways. The team also found large differences in iron abundance, a key ingredient in stellar winds and supernovae.
articles.summary: Hubble observations of massive metal-poor stars in dwarf galaxies provide crucial insights into why the early universe appears differently than expected.

articles.title: First stellar stream beyond the Milky Way could reveal dark matter
articles.description: Astronomers have discovered the first globular cluster stellar stream beyond the Milky Way, opening a new way to study dark matter in distant galaxies. These faint trails of stars trace a galaxy’s gravitational structure and could eventually help scientists map invisible matter across the universe.
articles.summary: Astronomers discover the first globular cluster stellar stream beyond the Milky Way, providing a novel observational tool to study dark matter distribution in other galaxies. This breakthrough opens new research pathways for understanding dark matter through tidal disruption patterns.

articles.title: China's FAST telescope to advance with Phase II construction as project marks 10th anniversary
articles.description: The Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Radio Telescope (FAST), known as the China's "Sky Eyes", will mark the 10th anniversary of its inauguration on September 25. Since its launch, the facility has achieved a series of landmark scientific and technologica…
articles.summary: China's FAST radio telescope marks its 10th anniversary and advances to Phase II construction, expanding its capabilities for astronomical discovery. This milestone celebrates a decade of groundbreaking observations and signals continued progress in global radio astronomy.

articles.title: Meet Julian Shapiro, the New York student who found 3 unusual dwarf galaxies and won $25,000
articles.description: Eighteen-year-old Julian Shapiro discovered three isolated dwarf galaxies that lack ongoing star formation, a puzzling combination for astronomers. His research suggests they could be “backsplash” galaxies that once passed near a massive galaxy, lost star-for…
articles.summary: Eighteen-year-old Julian Shapiro discovered three unusual isolated dwarf galaxies lacking active star formation, winning recognition and a $25,000 prize for his contribution to astronomical science. This inspiring achievement highlights how citizen science and young researchers continue advancing our understanding of galaxy evolution.

articles.title: La NASA selecciona PRIMA para la Fase B: el telescopio apunta a 2033
articles.description: La NASA seleccionó a PRIMA para avanzar a la Fase B de desarrollo y la misión apunta a lanzar el telescopio infrarrojo en 2033. El proyecto tiene un límite de costo de USD $1.200 millones, sin incluir el lanzamiento, y prevé adaptar un criorefrigerador de rep…
articles.summary: NASA selects the PRIMA infrared telescope mission to advance to Phase B development, targeting a 2033 launch date. This milestone represents progress toward a next-generation space observatory for infrared astronomy.
